You must adopt a little of my philosophy. Dwell upon the past only when remembering it affords you pleasure.”

“I cannot allow you the credit of such philosophy. Your recollections must be so entirely free from self-reproach that their resulting satisfaction comes not from philosophy, but from something far better, ignorance. With me, however, the case is different. Distressing memories force themselves upon me, and neither can nor ought to be driven away. All my life I have been selfish in conduct, though not in principle. In childhood I learned what was right, but never learned to govern my temper. Good principles were bestowed on me, yet I was left to practise them with pride and self-conceit. Unhappily an only son, and for many years an only child, I was indulged by my parents. Though themselves good, and my father especially everything kind and amiable, they permitted, encouraged, almost instructed me to be selfish and imperious; to regard nobody beyond my family circle; to hold the rest of mankind cheaply; at least to wish to hold their understanding and merit cheap beside my own. So I remained from eight years old to eight-and-twenty; and so I might have remained still, without you, my dearest, loveliest Elizabeth! How much I owe you! You gave me a lesson, painful at first indeed, yet most beneficial. Through you I was humbled as I ought to have been. I approached you perfectly certain of my welcome. You made me perceive how little all my claims could do to please a woman who deserved to be pleased.”

“Had you really convinced yourself that I should?”

“I certainly had. What must you think of my conceit? I imagined that you desired and awaited my proposals.”

“My behaviour must have been wrong, though quite unintentionally, I assure you. I had no wish to mislead you, but my high spirits may often have carried me astray. How you must have detested me after that evening!”

“Detest you! At first I was perhaps angry, but that anger soon began to find its proper object.”

“I scarcely dare ask what you thought of me at our meeting at Pemberley. Did you blame me for being there?”

“Indeed not; I was merely surprised.”

“You cannot have been more surprised than I was to receive your notice. My conscience assured me I merited no unusual civility, and I own I never expected more than I deserved.”

“My purpose then,” Darcy answered, “was to convince you, through every courtesy I could offer, that I was above resenting what had passed. I hoped to win your pardon and soften your unfavourable opinion by showing that I had listened to your rebukes.

I know so very little, and it vexes me—just a little.”

“Tell me what troubles you.”

“I have a cousin, my sole relation, and an orphan as I am, whom I love with all my heart. She is five years my junior, and lives at a farmer’s house in the southern country. Poverty separated us, and she does not know my fate—for I cannot write—and even if I could, how could I tell her! Things are better as they stand.”

“Yes, yes; better as they stand.”

“What has occupied my thoughts along the way, and occupies them still as I gaze at your kind, steadfast face, which sustains me so much, is this: if the Republic truly benefits the poor, and they grow less hungry and suffer less in every respect, she may live for many years; she may even reach old age.”

“And then, my gentle sister?”

“Do you suppose”—the patient eyes, with all their uncomplaining endurance, brim with tears, and the lips open a little wider and quiver—“that the time will seem long to me as I wait for her in that better country where I trust you and I will both find merciful shelter?”

“It cannot, my child; there is no Time in that place, and no sorrow.”

“You give me such comfort! I understand so little. Shall I kiss you now? Has the time arrived?”

“Yes.”

She kisses his lips, and he kisses hers; solemnly they bless one another. The thin hand is steady when he lets it go; the patient face holds nothing more grievous than sweet and shining resolution. She passes before him next—is gone; the women at their knitting reckon Twenty-Two.

“I am the Resurrection and the Life, says the Lord: whoever believes in me shall live, though he were dead; and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die.”

The murmur of innumerable voices, the lifting of innumerable faces, the crowding of footsteps at the edges of the throng, making it surge forward together like a mighty swell of water, all vanish in a flash. Twenty-Three.

*****

That night throughout the city people said his face had been the most peaceful man’s face ever seen there. Many said, besides, that his look was sublime and prophetic.

Not long before, among the most remarkable victims of that same axe, a woman had begged at the foot of that same scaffold for leave to set down the thoughts that inspired her. Had he spoken his own thoughts aloud, and had they been prophetic, they would have run thus:

“I see Barsad and Cly, Defarge, The Vengeance, the Juryman and the Judge, long files of new tyrants who have mounted upon the ruin of the old, dying beneath this avenging instrument before its present employment comes to an end.

The chain of necessity, perpetually producing misery, must have snapped, and the evil destiny that rules it would never suffer such a violation of her everlasting laws. Yet why should I lament this? Wretchedness was my native element, and only the wretched could come near me; had Woodville been happy, I should never have met him. And I, who for years was sustained by tears and nurtured beneath the dew of sorrow, can I hesitate to recount a history of anguish and death?

Woodville was compelled to travel into the country, where day after day he was detained in a weary separation from his beautiful bride. A letter came from her saying that she was a little unwell, but bidding him hurry home: his eyes would restore her health, and his presence would prove her surest medicine. Three further days detained him before he sped back to her. For reasons he could not explain, his heart foretold disaster; no second letter had arrived; he feared her illness had increased, and that fear made him restless and impatient for the instant when he would again behold her standing before him in her health and loveliness. For a sinister voice seemed continually to murmur, “You shall never see her again as she was.”

On reaching her dwelling he found everything silent. He passed through several chambers; in one a servant was weeping bitterly. Almost fainting with terror, he could scarcely utter, “Is she dead?” and barely heard the dreadful reply, “Not yet.” Appalling as these words were, they seemed less terrible than the answer he had anticipated; the knowledge that she still existed, that hope was still possible, brought him some relief. Recalling what she had written, he yielded to the wild fancy that his kisses, breathing warmth and love and life, would pour fresh spirit into her; that she could not die while he was beside her; that his presence was the charm preserving her life.

He hurried into her sick chamber. She lay with fever flaming in her cheeks, but with her eyes shut, apparently unconscious. He folded her within his arms and pressed breathless kisses on her hot lips. In a voice of restrained agony he called her by the most loving names: “Come back, Elinor; I am here beside you, your life, your love. Come back, my dearest; you promised me this blessing, that I should restore your health. Let your gentle spirit awaken; you cannot die with me near you. What is death? Never to look upon you again? To be divided from what forms part of my own being, without whom I possess neither remembrance nor a future?
